pages.title: Disclaimer
pages.summary: Not medical advice. First-aid pages are waiting on clinical review. Never eat a plant on one identification.
pages.html:
Not medical advice. Not legal advice. Not a rescue service.

The long form is DISCLAIMER.md in the repository. The short form is this:

If someone is badly hurt, confused, not breathing normally, or getting worse, contact local emergency services. Poison Control in the United States is 1-800-222-1222.

First-aid pages are drafts. Each one has `review: pending-clinical` until a licensed clinician, the pharmacist who owns this project, signs off. They cite CDC, Ready.gov, NPS, NIH MedlinePlus, and public Red Cross pages, and they link to Stop the Bleed. They do not give drug doses.

Never eat a wild plant on a single identification. This guide does not cover mushrooms. Poison hemlock, water hemlock, death camas, and yew are plants to avoid.

Hunting, fishing, and trapping rules are local. A page in this guide does not make a method legal.

Boil untreated water 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 6,500 feet, which is the CDC rule used here. Older pamphlets that say something else were not followed when they conflicted.

The guide is a static site. After the first load it is meant to work with the network off. It does not phone home.

pages.title: Arctic tundra
pages.summary: Stub for the Arctic. Cold injury and treated meltwater. Do not expect the eastern plant list to hold.
pages.html:
This is a stub. Tundra does not offer a debris hut's worth of leaves. FM 3-05.70's snow trench, snow cave, and snow mound are the shelter shapes when snow is deep enough. Vent any cave. Insulate yourself from the snow. Wind is the exposure FEMA ranks ahead of food.

CDC's hypothermia page is the care reference and it is a clinical draft. Frostbite cautions on that page matter here: do not rub frozen skin, and do not thaw it on a stove.

Melt ice in preference to eating snow, then boil. Elevation still changes the boil time if you are above 6,500 feet.

CDC's trichinellosis outbreak report says freeze-resistant Trichinella is a northern problem and that freezing game, including meat frozen for weeks, did not make bear meat safe. Cook wild game to at least 165°F. That is the cooking page, not a suggestion to hunt. Follow territorial and state law. Alaska subsistence rules are not this card.

Dandelion is recorded in Alaska by FEIS. Most of the fruit and nut cards are not tundra plants. Do not force them. Never eat on a single identification. Polar bear liver and similar high-vitamin organ stories are not in the sources used here, so they are not repeated.

pages.title: Boreal and taiga
pages.summary: Stub for northern conifer forest. Cold and wet are the first problems. Snow shelters need a vent.
pages.html:
This is a stub for the northern conifer belt. It does not invent a temperature normal.

FM 3-05.70's snow trench, snow cave, tree-pit, and snow-mound variation are the shelter tools when the snow is deep. Keep a ventilation shaft in a cave or mound. Insulate your body from the snow. CDC says hypothermia also happens above 40°F when you are wet. The hypothermia page is a clinical draft. Read it as draft guidance and get help if someone is confused or shivering and exhausted.

Boil meltwater. The snowmelt page says not to eat raw snow, then to treat the water. Above 6,500 feet the boil is 3 minutes. Much of the boreal forest is below that elevation. Use the elevation you are actually at, not the biome name.

Plant cards that tag this biome include raspberry, lowbush blueberry, and nettle where the range statements overlap. Berries are seasonal. Conifer needles are not a tea in this guide. Yew is on the flora rules page because it is deadly.

Biting insects are a nuisance and a disease path. Ticks are covered on the bites page. Do not eat them.

pages.title: Desert Southwest
pages.summary: Stub for hot, dry country. Shade and treated water come before food.
pages.html:
This is a stub. FM 3-05.70's desert shade is the shelter: a sheet anchored on a rock outcrop or a sand mound, or a trench above the high-water mark with a roof of poles. Washes flood. Do not camp in them because the sky is clear when you lie down.

Heat illness is the medical risk NIOSH describes: heat stroke is an emergency, and you cool the person while you get help. That page is a clinical draft. Do not wait for sweat to stop before you take confusion seriously. NIOSH says heat stroke skin can be dry or still sweating.

Water you find in the desert is still water CDC says to treat, unless it is a posted potable tap. Springs are not automatically safe. The dew and sheet-still page is a small backup, and boiling is still the surest germ kill. Do not drink water that may hold metals or farm chemicals. Boiling will not fix that.

This edition's plant cards are thin in the hottest deserts on purpose. Raspberry reaches Arizona in the FEIS range, which is not the same as "every desert shrub is food." There is no cactus-eating card. An older FEMA appendix says all cactus is safe. This guide does not use that sentence.

Solar disinfection is a sunny-climate backup on the water page. It takes hours and clear bottles. It is not a reason to skip a boil you can do.

pages.title: Eastern deciduous forest
pages.summary: Stub for the broadleaf forests of eastern North America. Start with site hazards and the eastern plant cards.
pages.html:
This is a stub. It does not add rainfall totals or a plant list beyond the cards that tag this biome.

The National Park Service camping page applies in these woods: look up for dead branches, stay out of ravines that flood, and do not camp on a peak or in the middle of a field in a lightning storm. Sequoia and Kings Canyon's hazard-tree warning is about western parks, and the same behavior is the right one under eastern hardwoods. Branches fall with or without wind.

Water is still treated. Clear creeks in deciduous forest are the kind of water CDC says can look safe and not be. Use the water module.

Plant cards tagged for this biome include white oak, black walnut, shagbark hickory, pawpaw, lowbush blueberry, and others. Open the plants module with this biome selected. Never eat on a single identification. The hemlock and yew rules are national, not regional.

Winter in the northern part of this forest is a shelter problem first. The debris hut and the lean-to are the builds that use leaves and a tarp. Snow shelters are for the boreal, alpine, and tundra stubs when the snow is deep enough for the Army methods.

pages.title: Great Plains
pages.summary: Stub for the plains. Wind, lightning, and sudden cold matter more than a view.
pages.html:
This is a stub. The plains are open, so the Park Service warning about lightning in the middle of a field and on high points is the site rule. Do not be the tallest object. The FEMA appendix says to put shelter on the lee side of the weather and out of washes and depressions. A dry creek in grassland is still a flood path.

Wind is the shelter problem. A low lean-to or a debris hut in a coulee that is not a flood channel beats a tall tent on a ridge. Ground insulation still matters. The plains get cold enough for hypothermia when you are wet. That care page is a clinical draft.

Water is often scarce and still needs treatment when you find it. Stock tanks and ditches can hold chemicals or algae. CDC says you cannot boil fuel or toxins out of water. If it smells like fuel or a chemical, leave it.

Dandelion is documented across the United States, including the plains states on the FEIS list. Cattail is a wetland plant, not a prairie-wide one. Use the biome filter. Never eat on a single identification.

Trapping and hunting follow the state. The legality page does not change because the land looks empty.

pages.title: Gulf and Southeast subtropical
pages.summary: Stub for the hot, humid Southeast and Gulf. Heat illness, storms, and treated water.
pages.html:
This is a stub for the humid Southeast and Gulf Coast. It does not add a hurricane procedure. If local authorities give an evacuation order, follow it. This guide is not a storm desk.

Heat is the NIOSH problem: heat stroke needs 911 and rapid cooling, and that page is a clinical draft. Humidity does not make the signs optional. Drink treated water on a schedule when you are working in the heat, and do not wait until you are confused.

The Park Service site rules still hold. Coastal and river country floods. Do not camp in a low spot because the ground is soft. Look up for dead limbs after storms. Widowmakers are not only a mountain problem.

Snakes are a NIOSH topic on the bites page. Do not cut a bite or put ice on it. Get emergency care. Alligators and other coastal hazards are not given a handling method here. Leave them alone.

Black cherry and pawpaw tag parts of this region in their FEIS ranges. Shagbark hickory is largely absent from the Gulf coastal plain in the FEIS review, so that card is not tagged here. Shellfish on the coast can carry toxins that cooking does not destroy. Read the fish page before you collect anything from a closed bed.

Water from a swamp still gets boiled or otherwise treated. CDC is clear that clear water can be unsafe, and swamp water is not even clear.

pages.title: Pacific Northwest temperate rainforest
pages.summary: Stub for the wet west-coast forest. Rain and dead wood overhead are the daily hazards.
pages.html:
This is a stub for the wet conifer forests of the Pacific Northwest. It does not add a rainfall number.

You will be wet. CDC says hypothermia happens above 40°F when rain or sweat soaks you. The hypothermia page is a clinical draft. Shelter priorities say dry ground insulation and a roof before a fire. A tarp lean-to with the back to the weather, and a debris hut if you can find dry litter under logs, are the builds.

Look up. The Park Service says not to camp under dead branches, and the Sequoia hazard page says trees fall in still air too. Big western trees make big widowmakers. Do not pitch in a debris-torrent channel.

Water is everywhere and still untreated. Boil it. The 3-minute rule is for elevations above 6,500 feet, which is a mountain number, not a rainforest number. Use your actual elevation.

Serviceberry and raspberry tag this biome where their FEIS ranges say so. Blue elderberry is the western riparian card from the USDA guide, with the red-berry warning. Never eat on a single identification. Mushrooms are not in this guide, including the ones that carpet these woods.

pages.title: Rockies alpine
pages.summary: Stub for high mountains. Wind, lightning, altitude boils, and avalanches.
pages.html:
This is a stub. The Park Service says not to stay on ledges or high peaks when wind and lightning are the hazard, and to stay off cliff edges. FM 3-05.70 says to avoid avalanche and rockslide paths. A snow cave dug in an avalanche path is not a shelter. It is a burial.

Above 6,500 feet, CDC says to boil water for 3 minutes, not 1. Much of the alpine Rockies is above that line. Melt snow before you drink it, then boil the melt. Do not eat raw snow.

Snow shelters in the Army manual need a ventilation shaft and a sleeping platform above the entrance. Tree-pits only work where the tree is alive enough not to be a hazard tree and bushy enough to help. Timberline may not give you that tree. Use the trench or the mound method if the snow allows, and do not invent a quinzhee diameter the manual does not print.

Serviceberry's FEIS range includes Colorado and Utah. That is not a reason to eat the first shrub with a dark fruit. Use the card. Hypothermia and heat both occur in the mountains, sometimes on the same day. Both care pages are clinical drafts.

pages.title: Cooking temperatures and parasites
pages.summary: Fish 145°F. Poultry 165°F. For wild game, CDC's trichinellosis work uses 165°F. Freezing does not reliably make wild game safe.
pages.html:
Use a food thermometer in the thickest part. These are the public numbers, including where they are not identical.

The charts

USDA FSIS safe minimums:

  • Fish and shellfish: 145°F (62.8°C).
  • All poultry, including ground poultry and whole birds: 165°F (73.9°C).
  • Ground meats (beef, pork, lamb, veal on that chart): 160°F (71.1°C).

FoodSafety.gov adds rabbit and venison, wild or farm-raised, at 160°F (71°C). It matches fish at 145°F, or until the flesh is opaque and flakes.

Wild game and Trichinella

CDC says the way to prevent trichinellosis is to cook meat to a safe internal temperature and not to sample it while it is raw. The animals it names as a risk include bear, wild boar, wildcat, fox, wolf, seal, and walrus, and undercooked pork. Curing, drying, smoking, or microwaving alone does not reliably kill the worms. Freezing pork has a CDC method (less than 6 inches thick, 20 days at 5°F / −15°C). Freezing wild game may not work, because some worms in wild game are freeze-resistant.

CDC's report on the 2022 bear-meat outbreak says cooking wild game to at least 165°F (74°C) is necessary to kill Trichinella, that the meat had been frozen for weeks and was still infectious, and that color is not a test of doneness. Vegetables cooked in the same pan as the rare meat also made people sick. Keep raw meat and its juice off other food.

Where FoodSafety.gov says 160°F for rabbit and venison and CDC's outbreak report says 165°F for wild game, this guide uses 165°F for wild mammals. Missouri's rabbit page also says at least 165°F because of tularemia. Poultry stays at the FSIS 165°F. Fish stays at 145°F, which is also CDC's anisakiasis cooking temperature.

What cooking does not fix

Shellfish toxins are not destroyed by cooking or freezing. That is the CDC Yellow Book line on the fish page. A sick animal is not made safe by a higher number. Do not eat it.

No antibiotic and no antiparasitic dose belongs on this page. If you are sick after a meal, get medical care and say what you ate.

pages.title: Field dressing
pages.summary: Gloves on, guts out and away from the meat, brain and spine left alone, carcass kept cool.
pages.html:
This is food-handling, not a hunting lesson. New York State's game page and CDC's tularemia page agree on the protective habits.

  • Wear gloves. Nitrile, rubber, or latex are the examples New York gives. CDC stresses gloves for rabbits, muskrats, prairie dogs, and other rodents. Bare hands with cuts are a bad combination with blood.
  • Do not eat, drink, or smoke while you are cleaning the animal.
  • Get the intestines out and do not puncture them. Keep intestinal contents off the meat. Discard the guts away from water you will treat and away from camp.
  • Look at a rabbit liver. Missouri says numerous pinhead white spots are a reason to throw the rabbit out and not eat it.
  • Remove bullets, slugs, shot, and the bruised meat around them.
  • Do not cut through the skull or the spinal cord. New York says to avoid brain, spinal tissue, saliva, and mouth parts. That is a rabies and chronic-wasting precaution. CDC says not to handle an animal that was acting sick. If it was, do not turn it into food. Get medical care if you were bitten or scratched.
  • Wash hands, knife, and the work surface with soap and water when you finish. New York also describes a bleach rinse for tools. Keep a knife you use on carcasses separate from the knife you use on food that is ready to eat.
  • Keep the carcass cool. New York says ice or refrigeration below 45°F (7°C) until it is butchered, then refrigerate or freeze until you cook it. In hot weather that means shade and speed, not a day in a pack.

Wash water is still untreated surface water until you treat it. Do not rinse a carcass in the creek you drink from and then skip the water pages.

Cooking temperatures are on the next page. Field dressing does not make rare meat safe.

pages.title: Fish
pages.summary: Cook fish to 145°F. Do not eat it raw. Shellfish toxins are not destroyed by cooking.
pages.html:
Fish is food only after it is cooked, and only if you may legally take it. Seasons, gear, and licenses are set by the state or province. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says that in most cases you need a hunting or fishing license from the state where you are, and that you have to follow that state's rules. This page does not list those rules.

USDA FSIS says cook fish and shellfish to a minimum internal temperature of 145°F (62.8°C). FoodSafety.gov says the same 145°F (63°C) for fish, or cook until the flesh is no longer translucent and separates with a fork. Use a food thermometer if you have one. Color alone is a weak test.

CDC's anisakiasis page says not to eat raw or undercooked fish or squid. People get the parasite from those dishes. The prevention line there is to cook seafood to an internal temperature of at least 145°F (about 63°C). Freezing can kill parasites under the conditions CDC prints: −4°F (−20°C) or below for 7 days, or −31°F (−35°C) until solid and then held at that temperature for 15 hours, or −31°F until solid and then −4°F for 24 hours. A camp cooler is not those conditions. Cook the fish.

Shellfish are a different problem. CDC's Yellow Book says marine shellfish toxins, including the toxin in paralytic shellfish poisoning, are not destroyed by stomach acid, canning, cooking, freezing, pickling, salting, or smoking. Avoid shellfish from waters during or just after harmful algal blooms, including what people call red tide. Cooking will not fix that. If a state has closed a beach or a shellfish bed, stay out of it.

Gut fish away from camp water, and treat the water you wash with. The water pages still apply.

This page does not list those rules. USDA FSIS says cook fish and shellfish to a minimum internal temperature of 145°F (62.8°C). FoodSafety.gov says the same 145°F (63°C) for fish, or cook until the flesh is no longer translucent and separates with a fork. Use a food thermometer if you have one. Color alone is a weak test. CDC's anisakiasis page says not to eat raw or undercooked fish or squid. People get the parasite from those dishes. The prevention line there is to cook seafood to an internal temperature of at least 145°F (about 63°C). Freezing can kill parasites under the conditions CDC prints: −4°F (−20°C) or below for 7 days, or −31°F (−35°C) until solid and then held at that temperature for 15 hours, or −31°F until solid and then −4°F for 24 hours. A camp cooler is not those conditions. Cook the fish. Shellfish are a different problem. CDC's Yellow Book says marine shellfish toxins, including the toxin in paralytic shellfish poisoning, are not destroyed by stomach acid, canning, cooking, freezing, pickling, salting, or smoking. Avoid shellfish from waters during or just after harmful algal blooms, including what people call red tide. Cooking will not fix that. If a state has closed a beach or a shellfish bed, stay out of it. Gut fish away from camp water, and treat the water you wash with. The water pages still apply.

pages.title: Insects
pages.summary: This guide does not name insects as safe to eat. Ticks are disease vectors, not food.
pages.html:
Insects are not a recommended food in the public pages this guide relies on. A FEMA training appendix says insects are edible and that flesh should be cooked. That line is broad enough to be dangerous, and this guide does not repeat it as permission. There is no USDA food-safety page in the sources here that names a North American insect species as a safe ration.

Do not eat ticks. CDC's tick page is about disease, including the need to remove attached ticks promptly. Tularemia prevention includes avoiding tick and deer-fly bites. A tick is a vector, not a snack. Do not eat flies off a carcass, and do not eat insects found on a sick or dead animal.

If you are considering any insect despite that, this card still has no species list and no "bright color" rule, because those rules are not in the cited pages. Cooking temperatures on the FSIS chart are for fish, poultry, and meat, not for a named insect. Do not invent a temperature and call it USDA.

Spend the effort on the plant cards you can actually match, or on getting help. Hunger is real. A wrong insect is not the fix this edition will pretend to teach.

pages.title: Small game
pages.summary: Rabbits and other small mammals can carry tularemia and rabies. Cook thoroughly and do not handle sick animals.
pages.html:
Small game means animals a state defines as small game: often rabbit, squirrel, and similar species. What is legal, and in which month, is not national. The Fish and Wildlife Service says you generally need the license of the state you are in and must follow that state's seasons and methods. Read them before you hunt. This page is about disease, not about how to evade a warden.

CDC says tularemia spreads through tick and deer-fly bites, contact with infected animals, contaminated water, and dust. Hunters should use gloves when handling animals, especially rabbits, muskrats, prairie dogs, and other rodents, and should cook game meat thoroughly. Do not handle animals that are sick or already dead if you do not have to. The Missouri Department of Conservation says to wear gloves while cleaning rabbits, to look at the liver, and to discard a rabbit with many pinhead-sized white spots on the liver. It says to cook rabbit to at least 165°F.

FoodSafety.gov lists rabbit and venison, wild or farm-raised, at 160°F (71°C). CDC's 2022 trichinellosis investigation says cooking wild game to at least 165°F (74°C) is what kills Trichinella, and that color is not a doneness test. When those numbers differ, use 165°F for wild mammals and use a thermometer. The cooking page explains the two citations side by side.

Rabies: CDC says not to approach wildlife that looks injured, sick, or dead. Raccoons, skunks, bats, and foxes are the usual reservoirs named on that page. Do not eat an animal that was acting sick. A bite or scratch is a medical emergency, not a meal.

Birds that are legal game are poultry once they are in the pot. FSIS says all poultry goes to 165°F. That is on the cooking page too.

pages.title: Trapping and hunting law
pages.summary: Seasons, gear, and licenses are set by the state or province. This guide does not teach you to ignore them.
pages.html:
Trapping and hunting are legal only inside the rules of the place you are standing. Those rules are not the same in Maine and Arizona, and they are not the same in a Canadian province as in the state across the border.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says that in most cases you need a hunting license from the state where the hunt happens, and you must follow that state fish and wildlife agency's requirements. Licenses are sold through state systems and many sporting-goods outlets. Every state writes its own seasons. Look them up before you go. A license from last year, or from a different state, is not a guess you should test.

On national wildlife refuges, the Service says trapping has to follow state laws, state regulations, and state licensing, and some refuges also require a special-use permit. Some refuges do not allow public trapping even when state land nearby does. Alaska subsistence rules are a separate statute. Read the refuge sheet, not a forum post.

This page does not describe how to build a trap, a snare, or a deadfall. Those methods are regulated as equipment. Describing a trap here would not tell you whether it is legal in your county this month. If you trap, use the current regulations booklet from the state or province, take the required education course, and use only the devices that booklet allows.

Provinces run their own systems. A U.S. federal page will not answer a provincial season. Check the provincial wildlife agency.

Poaching is not a survival technique this project will write down. If you are lost, the shelter and water pages are the immediate work. Food can wait longer than exposure.

pages.title: Bites and stings
pages.summary: Snakebite needs emergency care. Do not cut, suck, ice, or tourniquet it. Remove a tick with tweezers.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE.

Venomous snake

NIOSH says to get emergency care as soon as possible so antivenom can be started if it is needed. Do not drive yourself if the bite can make you dizzy or pass out. A photo from a safe distance may help. Do not pick up the snake, including a dead one or a severed head.

While you wait:

  • Lay or sit with the bite in a neutral position of comfort.
  • Take off rings and watches before swelling starts.
  • Wash with soap and water.
  • Cover with a clean, dry dressing.
  • Mark the edge of tenderness or swelling and write the time next to it.

NIOSH says not to: wait for symptoms, apply a tourniquet, use electric shock or folk remedies, cut the wound, suck the venom, apply ice or soak the wound, drink alcohol as a painkiller, or take aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen. This page names those drugs only as items NIOSH says not to use. It does not give a dose of anything else.

Tick

CDC says to remove an attached tick as soon as you can. Do not wait for a clinic to do it.

  1. 1. Grasp the tick as close to the skin as you can with clean fine-tipped tweezers. Regular tweezers or fingers are the backup. Do not squeeze the body.
  2. 2. Pull upward with steady, even pressure. Do not twist or jerk. If the mouthparts break off and you cannot lift them easily, leave them. The skin pushes them out as it heals.
  3. 3. Kill the loose tick in alcohol, tape, a sealed container, or the toilet. Do not crush it in your fingers.
  4. 4. Clean the bite and your hands with soap and water, rubbing alcohol, or sanitizer.
  5. 5. Check the rest of the body. More than one tick is common.

Do not use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish, or other substances to make the tick let go. CDC says that can agitate the tick.

If a rash or fever shows up in the days to weeks after a bite, see a clinician and say when and where the tick bite happened. This guide does not give an antibiotic dose. Prophylaxis decisions are on CDC clinician pages and are not repeated here.

Mammals

CDC's rabies page says people in the United States are usually exposed by wild animals, commonly raccoons, skunks, bats, and foxes. Do not approach an animal that looks injured, sick, or dead, especially one that is out in daylight when that species is normally nocturnal. A bite or scratch needs medical care urgently. Do not try to catch the animal. Rabies care is time-sensitive and is not a field recipe in this guide.

pages.title: Bleeding control
pages.summary: Find the source and press hard until help arrives. A tourniquet is for life-threatening bleeding on an arm or leg.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE. Take a Stop the Bleed class if you can: stopthebleed.org. The steps below are the public Ready.gov sequence and a short paraphrase of the public Red Cross pages, not those courses.

Ready.gov's one-page card says:

  1. 1. Find the source of the bleeding. There may be more than one wound.
  2. 2. If you have something to put between the blood and your hands, use it. Gloves, a cloth, or a plastic bag are the examples on the card.
  3. 3. Apply firm, steady pressure directly on the source. Push hard, even if it hurts the person.
  4. 4. Keep that pressure until emergency medical services arrive.

The longer Ready.gov tutorial says a bandage alone soaks up blood. Pressure is what stops bleeding. Hold it until crews take over, and trade off with another person if your hands tire. Call for help. Move someone only to get them out of further danger.

The public Red Cross bleeding page says the urgent move is pressure right away, with hands or with cloth, and that life-threatening bleeding on an arm or leg can take a tourniquet if you have one and know how. It also says wound packing is for people who are trained, for life-threatening bleeding of the scalp, neck, shoulder, groin, or back, or of a limb when no tourniquet is available. This guide does not teach packing. Get the class.

Ready.gov describes a tourniquet as another way to put firm pressure on an arm or leg when the bleeding will not stop otherwise, and its quiz answer for a wound near the knee is to place the tourniquet above the wound. The public Red Cross tourniquet article says to place a commercial tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, between the wound and the heart, not on the wound and not on a joint, to follow the device instructions, and not to loosen or remove it. A medical professional does that. If the first tourniquet is as tight as it will go and the bleeding has not stopped, that article says a second one can go above the first, closer to the heart.

Do not wait to see if bleeding slows on its own when it is spurting or soaking through pressure. That is a reason to evacuate, and it is on the evacuate page.

This page does not give a time limit for how long a tourniquet may stay on, and it does not give a drug dose.

pages.title: Burns
pages.summary: Cool with cool water, not ice. Do not break blisters. Large, deep, chemical, and electrical burns need help.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE. Ready.gov is the source for this page.

Ready.gov describes three depths in plain language. First-degree burns affect the top layer of skin and may be red, swollen, and painful. Second-degree burns reach the thicker lower layer and may blister, swell, and hurt. Third-degree burns go through the skin into tissue underneath. Ready.gov says third-degree burns need immediate medical attention. The burned skin may be dry and leathery, with white, brown, or black patches.

For a minor burn, Ready.gov says:

  • Remove clothing, jewelry, and metal from the burned area. They hold heat. Do not peel off anything that is stuck.
  • Use cool water, not cold water and not ice. Ice can add injury.
  • Especially for a chemical burn, hold the skin under cool running water for 10 to 15 minutes, until it hurts less.
  • If you have no running water, use a cool clean wet cloth, or a cool bath for five minutes.
  • Clean gently with soap and water.
  • Do not break blisters. An open blister can get infected.
  • A thin layer of petroleum jelly or aloe vera is allowed on that page. The ointment does not need an antibiotic in it. Do not use cream, lotion, oil, cortisone, butter, or egg white.
  • Cover with sterile non-stick gauze that will not shed fibers. Change it once a day.

This guide does not name an antibiotic ointment and does not give a pain-medicine dose. Ready.gov's "when to get help" list is the evacuate rule for burns:

  • Dark red, glossy, and heavily blistered.
  • Larger than about two inches.
  • From fire, electricity, or chemicals.
  • Dry and leathery, or with white, brown, or black patches.
  • Signs of infection: more pain, redness, swelling, discharge, fever, swollen lymph nodes, or a red streak.

Ready.gov also says burns are susceptible to tetanus, and that a person whose last tetanus shot was more than five years ago may need a booster. That decision is a clinician's. Do not guess a vaccine dose in the field.

pages.title: When to evacuate
pages.summary: Leave or call for help for bleeding you cannot stop, heat stroke, serious cold injury, snakebite, and a deformed or numb limb.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE. "Evacuate" here means get to emergency care, or get care to you. It does not mean walk out if walking will kill you. Call first when you have a signal. Move a person only to get them out of further danger, which is the Ready.gov order.

Go now, or call now, if any of these are true. Each line is from the page cited.

  • Bleeding that spurts or that you cannot stop with firm direct pressure. Ready.gov treats that as a reason to keep pressure until EMS arrives, and to use a tourniquet on an arm or leg when pressure will not stop it.
  • Hypothermia signs, or a measured temperature below 95°F. CDC calls that an emergency. An unconscious cold person needs emergency help even if you are not sure you feel a pulse.
  • Heat stroke signs: confusion, seizure, loss of consciousness, or a very high temperature. NIOSH says call 911 and cool the person while you wait. Heat exhaustion also goes to a clinic, and to 911 if no clinic exists.
  • Any venomous-snake bite. NIOSH says do not wait for symptoms.
  • A burn that is larger than about two inches, heavily blistered, leathery or patchy white, brown, or black, or caused by chemicals or electricity. Ready.gov.
  • A limb that is bent wrong, has bone showing, has lost feeling or a pulse, or has blue numb fingers or toes. MedlinePlus.
  • A tick bite followed by rash or fever. CDC says see a doctor. That can often wait for the next clinic rather than a night march. Do not invent an antibiotic plan in camp.
  • A bite or scratch from a bat, raccoon, skunk, fox, or other wild mammal, or contact with a bat when a bite may have gone unnoticed. CDC says seek medical care urgently.

Do not start a long walk at the end of the day through terrain you cannot see, into a storm, or across a flood wash, if you can signal from where you are. The shelter and water pages still apply while you wait. Food is not the reason to move if the problems above are the reason you are moving.

Tell the responders what happened, what you did, and the time you put on a tourniquet if you used one. Do not take the tourniquet off to "check."

pages.title: Fractures and splinting
pages.summary: Do not straighten a broken limb. Splint it in the position you found it and get help.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE. Setting a bone is a clinician's job. MedlinePlus says not to straighten a bone or test whether it still moves. If you think the head, neck, or back is hurt, do not move the person except to get them out of immediate danger, and do not try to reposition a suspected spine injury.

MedlinePlus broken-bone first aid, paraphrased:

  • Check airway and breathing. Call emergency services and start CPR or bleeding control only if you are trained and it is needed.
  • Keep the person still and calm. Look for other injuries.
  • If help is coming soon, let them take the next steps.
  • If skin is broken, call for emergency help. Do not breathe on the wound or probe it. Cover it with a sterile dressing if you have one. Do not try to line the bone up unless you are medically trained to do so.
  • If you must immobilize, use a splint or sling. A rolled newspaper or strips of wood are the examples MedlinePlus gives. Immobilize above and below the injured bone.
  • Do not move a person with an injured hip, pelvis, or upper leg unless you have to. If you must, MedlinePlus says to pull them to safety by their clothes.

Splint

MedlinePlus "how to make a splint":

  • Care for an open wound before the splint. Rinse and cover it.
  • Splint in the position you found, unless a specialist has already treated that part.
  • Use something rigid: sticks, boards, rolled newspaper. A rolled blanket or clothing if that is all you have. You can tape an injured finger to the next finger.
  • Extend the splint past the injury. Include the joint above and the joint below when you can.
  • Tie with cloth, a belt, or tape above and below the injury. Knots should not sit on the injury. Do not tie tight enough to cut off circulation.
  • Pad the splint. Recheck for swelling, paleness, or numbness, and loosen it if those show up.
  • If the pain is worse after the splint, take the splint off and get medical help.

MedlinePlus also says that if you are remote, no help is available, the part looks abnormally bent, and the limb is pale, gently placing it back toward a normal position may improve circulation. That sentence is an exception on their page, not the default. Do not treat it as permission to haul on a joint. This draft flags it for the clinical reviewer. When help exists, do not realign.

Sling

For an arm, MedlinePlus says to splint first if a splint is needed, then sling. A triangular cloth works: elbow at the top point, wrist along the base, free ends tied at the neck, hand higher than the elbow, elbow near a right angle. Fingertips stay visible so you can see color. Remove watches and rings. Tie the arm to the chest if it must stay still. Loosen anything that makes the hand cool, pale, blue, numb, or tingling.

Get help for bone through the skin, an open wound, loss of feeling, loss of a pulse or of warmth, or fingers and toes that turn blue and numb. Those are MedlinePlus reasons to seek care right away.

Call emergency services and start CPR or bleeding control only if you are trained and it is needed. - Keep the person still and calm. pages.title: Heat illness
pages.summary: Heat stroke is an emergency. Cool the person fast. Heat exhaustion still needs rest, shade, and fluids.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE. The steps below are from NIOSH's heat-illness page for workers. They apply to anyone overheating outdoors.

Heat stroke

NIOSH says heat stroke is the most serious heat illness. The body can no longer control its temperature. Temperature can rise to 106°F or higher within 10 to 15 minutes. It can cause permanent disability or death if treatment is delayed.

Signs on that page: confusion, altered mental status, slurred speech, loss of consciousness, hot dry skin or profuse sweating, seizures, very high body temperature.

What NIOSH says to do:

  • Call 911.
  • Stay with the person.
  • Move them to shade or a cool place and remove outer clothing.
  • Cool them quickly. A cold-water or ice bath if you can. Wet the skin. Cold wet cloths. Soak clothing with cool water.
  • Fan them.
  • Cold wet cloths or ice on the head, neck, armpits, and groin, or soak the clothing.

Heat exhaustion

Signs: headache, nausea, dizziness, weakness, irritability, thirst, heavy sweating, elevated body temperature, less urine.

NIOSH says to get the person to a clinic or emergency room, and to call 911 if medical care is not available. Have someone stay with them. Move them out of the heat, remove extra clothing including shoes and socks, cool them with cold compresses or by washing the head, face, and neck with cold water, and encourage frequent sips of cool water.

Other heat problems on the same page

Heat cramps: muscle cramps or spasms. NIOSH says drink water and have a snack or a drink that replaces carbohydrates and electrolytes, such as a sports drink, every 15 to 20 minutes, and to avoid salt tablets. Get medical help if the person has heart problems, is on a low-sodium diet, or the cramps last more than an hour.

This guide does not turn "a sports drink" into a recipe or a salt dose.

Rhabdomyolysis can follow hard work in heat. NIOSH lists muscle pain, weakness, and urine the color of tea or cola. Stop, drink water, and get to medical care. Do not wait that one out in camp.

Heat rash: cool off, keep the skin dry. NIOSH says not to use ointments and creams on it.

Confusion plus a very hot body is heat stroke until a clinician says otherwise. That is an evacuate-now problem.

pages.title: Hypothermia and frostbite
pages.summary: Get the person dry and out of the wind. Warm the center of the body. A temperature under 95°F needs medical care.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE. Hypothermia is a medical emergency on the CDC winter page.

CDC says hypothermia can happen in very cold air, and also above 40°F if the person is wet from rain, sweat, or cold water. A low body temperature affects thinking, so the person may not know it is happening.

Adult warning signs on that page: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness. In babies: bright red, cold skin and very low energy. NIOSH lists late signs that include no shivering, blue skin, dilated pupils, slow pulse and breathing, and loss of consciousness. Shivering that stops is not a sign that the person is fine.

If you can take a temperature and it is below 95°F, CDC says to get medical attention immediately.

If you cannot get help right away, CDC says:

  • Get the person into a warm room or shelter.
  • Remove wet clothing.
  • Warm the center of the body — chest, neck, head, and groin — with an electric blanket if you have one, or with skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry layers.
  • Warm drinks can help if the person is conscious. Do not give alcohol. Do not try to give a drink to someone who is unconscious.
  • Once temperature has come up, keep them dry and wrapped, including head and neck, and still get medical care.

For severe hypothermia, CDC says the person may be unconscious and may not seem to have a pulse or to be breathing. Handle them gently, get emergency help, and give CPR even if they look dead, continuing until they respond or medical aid takes over. Keep warming them during CPR. This guide does not teach CPR. Use training you already have, and the emergency number.

Frostbite, from the same CDC page: do not walk on frostbitten feet unless you have to. Do not warm frostbite on a stove, radiator, heat lamp, fireplace, heating pad, or electric blanket. Do not rub it. CDC says to put the frostbitten area in warm-to-touch water, not hot water you cannot judge. Numb skin burns easily.

Shelter and dry layers are the prevention side. They are in the shelter module. This page is the care side, and it is still awaiting clinical review.

pages.summary: Not medical advice. These pages are drafts waiting on a clinician. No drug doses.
pages.html:
NOT MEDICAL ADVICE. This is not a diagnosis, a prescription, or a wilderness-medicine course. If someone is badly hurt, confused, having trouble breathing, or getting worse, contact local emergency services. In much of the United States and Canada that number is 911. Poison Control in the United States is 1-800-222-1222.

Every page in this module is marked `review: pending-clinical`. A licensed pharmacist, the owner of this project, does a clinical last look before any first-aid page is treated as ready to ship. Until that review is written onto the page, read it as a draft that repeats public agency wording.

What these pages will not do:

  • They will not tell you a drug dose. There are no milligram amounts for pain medicine, antibiotics, or any other drug.
  • They will not copy Stop the Bleed or Red Cross course manuals. Those programs are linked so you can take the class.
  • They will not replace hands-on training. Bleeding control, CPR, and splinting are skills you practice before you need them.

What to do while you wait for help, from the public pages cited on the topic pages: stop dangerous bleeding with firm pressure, get a cold person out of wet clothes and wind, cool a person in heat stroke, and do not straighten a deformed limb. The evacuate page lists situations those same sources treat as emergencies.

pages.title: Saskatoon serviceberry
pages.summary: A western shrub or small tree with clustered berrylike pomes. The fruit is the food.
pages.season: When the pomes are ripe in the cluster
pages.name: Saskatoon serviceberry
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USFS serviceberry review used here
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes Saskatoon serviceberry as a native deciduous shrub or small tree, about 3 to 26 feet (1 to 8 m), often in thickets or clumps. Flowers and fruits are in terminal clusters. The fruits are berrylike pomes. Each fruit has 4 to 10 small seeds, and the seedcoat is leathery.

Season

Use ripe fruit. FEIS does not give a single calendar date. Unripe fruit is not what the food notes describe.

Range

FEIS says the species runs from east-central California north to southern Alaska, east to Ontario and southwestern Quebec, and south to southern Colorado and Utah. Varieties split that map. The typical variety is mostly east of the Cascades from southern Alaska to southern Oregon, and east to the Dakotas, Nebraska, and Colorado. Check PLANTS for the plant in your hand. Other Amelanchier species are not automatically this card.

Preparation

FEIS says the fruits are added to pastries and used for jelly or syrup, and that several cultivars are grown for fruit. Wash the pomes and cook them if you are not sure they are fully ripe and clean. The review also says Native Americans made a medicinal tea by boiling the branches. This guide does not teach that tea.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The FEIS review used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this plant on a single identification. You want the clustered pomes on this shrub, not a lone berry on a different plant. If you cannot match the cluster and the growth form, do not eat it.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Pawpaw
pages.summary: Eastern understory tree with large fruit. Eat the pulp. Do not eat the seeds. Handling the fruit can cause a rash in some people.
pages.season: When the large fruit is ripe
pages.name: Pawpaw
lookalikes: Seeds contain the alkaloid asiminine, which FEIS says is reported to have emetic properties
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes pawpaw as a native deciduous large shrub or small tree, about 20 to 40 feet (6 to 12 m), usually with a single trunk, growing in clones or thickets. Bark is thin with shallow irregular fissures. Young twigs are hairy. Leaves can be up to 1 foot (30 cm) long and smell when bruised. The fruit is a large berry. Flowers come out with the leaves.

Season

Eat ripe fruit. FEIS says flowers emerge with the leaves from February in the southern part of the seasonal note, but it does not give one ripening month for the whole range. A hard green fruit is not the food described.

Range

FEIS says pawpaw is widely distributed in the eastern United States: from western New York west across southwestern Ontario to Michigan, Illinois, and Iowa; south to eastern Nebraska, eastern Oklahoma, and eastern Texas; east to the Appalachians and the Florida panhandle. It grows in deciduous forests, on ravine slopes, and along streams.

Preparation

FEIS says people eat the fruit raw, cooked in puddings or breads, or used in ice cream. Eat the pulp. Handling the fruit may cause allergic reactions in sensitive people. If your skin reacts, stop handling it and wash. Do not eat the seeds or the bark.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

FEIS says the seeds contain an alkaloid, asiminine, reported to have emetic properties, and that the bark contains an alkaloid, analobine. The hazard named here is the plant's own seeds and bark, not a second species. Never eat this plant on a single identification. If the bruised leaf does not smell and the fruit is not the large berry on this clonal understory tree, do not eat it. This guide does not name another species as a pawpaw double because the review does not.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Shagbark hickory
pages.summary: Eastern hickory with bark in long shaggy plates. The nuts are sweet when they are the right tree.
pages.name: Shagbark hickory
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USFS shagbark review; other hickories are not this card
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes shagbark hickory as a medium to large deciduous tree, commonly 60 to 80 feet (20 to 25 m). Open-grown crowns are oblong. Forest trees tend toward a straighter, narrower crown. The gray bark exfoliates in long plate-like strips. That shag is the feature the common name is for. The tree is monoecious. The fruit is the nut. A smooth-barked hickory is not this species.

Season

Collect mature nuts. FEIS does not give a single calendar date for the whole range.

Range

FEIS says shagbark hickory occurs through most of eastern North America but is largely absent from the southeastern and Gulf coastal plains and the lower Mississippi Delta. It runs from southeastern Nebraska and southeastern Minnesota east through southern Ontario and Quebec to Maine, and south to Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and eastern Texas, with disjunct populations reported in the mountains of northeastern Mexico.

Preparation

FEIS says the nuts are sweet and edible, that they were a staple for some Native American peoples, and that they are the commercial hickory nut. Crack and eat the kernel. Discard insect-bored or moldy nuts. The bark plates are not food.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The FEIS review used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat a nut on a single identification. Other hickories grow in the same woods and are not automatically sweet. If the bark does not shed in the long plates FEIS describes, do not use this card. A nut you cannot match to the tree stays on the ground.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Common persimmon
pages.summary: A deciduous eastern tree. Eat ripe fruit only. Do not eat the seeds.
pages.season: Ripe fruit. Unripe fruit is not the food described here.
pages.name: Common persimmon
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USFS persimmon review; unripe fruit is not the food use
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes common persimmon as a slow-growing, thicket-forming, dioecious deciduous tree, up to 70 feet (21 m) and generally under 40 feet (12 m), with a rounded or conical crown. Leaves are simple, alternate, entire, and elliptical to oblong. The fruit is a persistent spherical berry with one to eight flat seeds. Flowers bloom from March onward on the seasonal note in that review. Match leaf, fruit, and growth form together.

Season

FEIS says ripe fruit can be eaten. It mentions unripe fruit only in a medicinal context this guide will not teach. Wait until the fruit is ripe. If it is still hard and astringent, it is not ready.

Range

Use the FEIS review and the USDA PLANTS map for the stand in front of you. The species is an eastern U.S. tree in that review's community lists. This card does not add a state list the extracted review section did not print as a clean range sentence.

Preparation

FEIS says ripe fruit can be eaten raw, cooked, or dried. Spit out or remove the seeds. They are not described as food. The review's notes on unripe fruit and inner bark for fever, diarrhea, and hemorrhage are medicinal and are not instructions here.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The FEIS review used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this plant on a single identification. Eat only ripe fruit from a tree that matches the leaf and berry above. Do not eat seeds, bark, or unripe fruit from this card. If the fruit is not the persistent spherical berry on this tree, leave it.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Virginia strawberry
pages.summary: A low perennial with three leaflets and a red fruit dotted with seeds. Eat the fruit.
pages.season: When the red fruit is ripe
pages.name: Virginia strawberry
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USDA strawberry guide used here
pages.html:
Identification

The USDA NRCS plant guide (symbol FRVI) describes Fragaria virginiana as a herbaceous perennial in the rose family. It spreads by seed and by short rhizomes and leafless stolons. Leaves are toothed, thin, and basal, with a petiole generally 1 to 12 cm, in threes, and generally smooth above. Flowers have 5 white petals about 4 to 9 mm, numerous pistils, and 20 to 35 stamens. The five bractlets are unlobed. The fruit is red and fleshy, with achenes on the surface.

Season

Eat ripe red fruit. The guide does not give one month for the whole range. Flowers and fruit are not interchangeable. The guide notes that plants with bigger flowers may have less fruit.

Range

The guide says to check the PLANTS profile for the current map. The copy used here says the plant is found between about 1,200 and 3,300 m in meadows and forest openings, in the Klamath Ranges, high Cascade Range, Modoc Plateau, and Sierra Nevada, and to eastern North America. A strawberry in a city lawn may be a different cultivated plant. Match the features anyway.

Preparation

The guide says Indigenous peoples through parts of Canada picked and ate the fruit, and names Midwestern prairie and Great Lakes tribes, including the Omaha, Hidatsa, and Mandan, among people who used it. Wash the fruit and eat it ripe. Leaves are not described as the food on this card.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The USDA guide used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this plant on a single identification. You want all of these together: three leaflets, five white petals, unlobed bractlets, and a red fruit with the seeds on the surface. If the fruit is dry, white, or held differently, do not eat it from this card.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.
pages.text: ## Identification The USDA NRCS plant guide (symbol FRVI) describes *Fragaria virginiana* as a herbaceous perennial in the rose family. It spreads by seed and by short rhizomes and leafless stolons. Leaves are toothed, thin, and basal, with a petiole generally 1 to 12 cm, in threes, and generally smooth above. Flowers have 5 white petals about 4 to 9 mm, numerous pistils, and 20 to 35 stamens. The five bractlets are unlobed. The fruit is red and fleshy, with achenes on the surface. ## Season Eat ripe red fruit. The guide does not give one month for the whole range. Flowers and fruit are not interchangeable. The guide notes that plants with bigger flowers may have less fruit. ## Range The guide says to check the PLANTS profile for the current map. The copy used here says the plant is found between about 1,200 and 3,300 m in meadows and forest openings, in the Klamath Ranges, high Cascade Range, Modoc Plateau, and Sierra Nevada, and to eastern North America. A strawberry in a city lawn may be a different cultivated plant. Match the features anyway. ## Preparation The guide says Indigenous peoples through parts of Canada picked and ate the fruit, and names Midwestern prairie and Great Lakes tribes, including the Omaha, Hidatsa, and Mandan, among people who used it. Wash the fruit and eat it ripe. Leaves are not described as the food on this card. ## DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES The USDA guide used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this plant on a single identification. You want all of these together: three leaflets, five white petals, unlobed bractlets, and a red fruit with the seeds on the surface. If the fruit is dry, white, or held differently, do not eat it from this card. ## Rule Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Black walnut
pages.summary: Eastern tree. The nut is the food. The hull is not a snack.
pages.name: Black walnut
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USFS black walnut review used here
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes black walnut as a native deciduous tree, often around 80 feet (25 m) and capable of 125 feet (38 m). In the forest the trunk is long and the crown small. In the open the trunk forks low. Young bark is dark and scaly. Older bark is darker with rounded intersecting ridges. The nut is the food part the review names. Match the tree, not a lone nut on the ground that could have rolled from somewhere else.

Season

Harvest mature nuts. FEIS says flowering begins about mid-April in the southern part of its seasonal note. It does not give one drop date. Use nuts that are full, not moldy and not insect dust.

Range

FEIS says black walnut grows through the eastern United States, north to southern Minnesota, southern Wisconsin, southern Michigan, and southern Ontario, with isolated populations in southern New York, Vermont, western Massachusetts, and northwestern Connecticut, south to northwestern Florida and through Mississippi, Arkansas, and Louisiana except the Mississippi Valley and Delta, and with isolated Midwest populations in eastern Texas, western Oklahoma, and central Kansas.

Preparation

FEIS says people eat the nuts plain or with honey and use them to flavor cakes, candy, and ice cream, and that Native Americans used the nuts for food. Husk them, dry them, and crack the shell. The green hull stains skin and is not described as the food. A dye from the roots is also not food.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The FEIS review used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this nut on a single identification. If you cannot tie the nut to a black walnut tree with the bark and form above, do not eat it. Do not eat nuts that smell of mold.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Black cherry
pages.summary: Ripe fruit, pitted, is the only part this card treats as food. Leaves, bark, and seeds are not.
pages.season: When the fruit is ripe; eat the flesh only, with the pit removed
pages.name: Black cherry
lookalikes: Chokecherry and other Prunus are on the USDA cyanide-plant list; do not eat leaves, bark, or seeds
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes black cherry as a deciduous tree. In eastern forest it often has a straight, branch-free trunk and a narrow crown. In the open the trunk is shorter and the crown broader. Typical eastern trees (var. serotina) may reach 125 feet (38 m). Southwestern varieties are smaller. Mature bark is shown in the FEIS review as dark and plated. Confirm bark, leaves, and fruit together. This card does not reduce the tree to "a tree with cherries."

Season

Use ripe fruit. FEIS says pitted fruits are edible and are eaten raw and used in wine and jelly. It does not give one ripening date for every variety.

Range

FEIS says black cherry grows in eastern North America from western Minnesota south to eastern Texas and east to the Atlantic from central Florida to Nova Scotia, with outlying populations in central Texas, the mountains of western Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, and south in Mexico to Guatemala.

Preparation

Remove the pit. Eat or cook the flesh. Do not crush seeds into the jelly. FEIS notes the bark was used historically as a cough remedy. This guide does not teach bark medicine. There is no dose, and bark is not food.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

USDA ARS lists chokecherry (Prunus spp.) among cyanide-containing poisonous plants. Black cherry is a Prunus. Do not eat leaves, bark, or seeds. Wilted foliage is a known livestock hazard for this genus in that ARS grouping. Never eat this plant on a single identification. A cherry you cannot separate from another Prunus still follows the same limit: flesh of ripe fruit only, pits out, and only if you are sure of the tree. If you are not sure, do not eat it.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Chokecherry
pages.summary: Ripe fruit is used for jelly, jam, syrup, and wine. The plant is also a cyanide-containing Prunus.
pages.season: Fully ripe fruit only; the flesh, not the stone
pages.name: Chokecherry
lookalikes: USDA ARS lists chokecherry (Prunus) among cyanide-containing plants
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes chokecherry as a native deciduous shrub or small tree that forms thickets. Stems are numerous and slender. Height is often about 3 to 19.5 feet (1 to 6 m), sometimes taller. Flowers are on leafy twigs of the season. Fruits are drupes, each with a small stone.

Season

FEIS says the fruits are somewhat astringent and relatively sweet when fully ripe. Use fully ripe fruit. Unripe fruit is not the food described there.

Range

FEIS treats chokecherry as a widespread native shrub and discusses it in eastern, central, and western communities, including prairie and mountain plantings. Use the FEIS review and the USDA PLANTS map for the stand in front of you rather than a state guess from this card. The food rule does not change with the state: ripe flesh only.

Preparation

FEIS says fruits are used to make wines, syrups, jellies, and jams, and that Indigenous peoples gathered them. Remove the stones before you cook. Do not blend whole fruit. Do not eat the seeds.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

USDA ARS lists chokecherry (Prunus spp.) among plants that contain cyanide (prussic acid). Leaves, bark, and seeds are not food. Never eat this plant on a single identification. Black cherry is a related tree with the same limit, and it is a separate card. If you cannot tell them apart, you can still follow the shared rule, and you should not invent a third use. If the fruit is not a ripe drupe on this thicket-forming shrub, do not eat it.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: White oak
pages.summary: Eastern oak. Acorns were traditionally boiled to pull out bitter tannins. Do not eat the leaves.
pages.season: When mature acorns are on the tree or freshly fallen
pages.name: White oak
lookalikes: Oak itself is on the USDA poisonous-plant list for livestock; leaves and unprocessed acorns are not a raw meal
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes white oak as a medium to large deciduous tree, commonly 60 to 80 feet (18 to 24 m), taller on good sites. It is monoecious. Yellowish staminate catkins are at the base of new growth. Pistillate flowers are in the axils of new growth. Acorns are short-stalked, glabrous, ovoid, and tan to brown.

Season

Use mature acorns. FEIS does not give a single drop date for the whole range. Collect when the nuts are full and tan to brown, not when they are green mush.

Range

FEIS says white oak grows through much of the eastern United States, from southwest Maine to northern Florida, Alabama, and Georgia, west through southern Ontario and Quebec into the Great Lakes states and south to eastern Kansas, eastern Oklahoma, and eastern Texas. Confirm the tree on the USDA PLANTS map. Acorns from other oaks are not this card.

Preparation

FEIS says acorns were a traditional food for many Native American peoples. They have been described as sweet and edible and also as slightly bitter. They were often boiled to remove bitter tannins. Boil pieces in changes of water until the bitterness is gone, then cook them as a food. The review does not give a minute count. Taste is the check it implies by "bitter," and you still throw out nuts that are moldy or insect-hollow. This card does not teach acorn oil as a pain treatment. That medicinal line in FEIS is not a field dose.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

USDA ARS lists oak (Quercus) among poisonous plants. Livestock are poisoned by oak browse. Do not eat leaves, buds, or bark. Do not eat raw acorns and call them finished. Never eat an acorn on a single identification of the tree. If you cannot show that the tree is a white oak, do not use this card for its nuts. This guide does not name a second species as a look-alike beyond that limit, because the FEIS review does not.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: American red raspberry
pages.summary: A bristly cane with leaves in threes or fives and an aggregate red fruit. Eat the ripe fruit.
pages.season: When the fruit is ripe on the cane
pages.name: American red raspberry
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USFS raspberry review used here
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes American red raspberry as a deciduous, erect or arching, thicket-forming shrub about 1.6 to 9.8 feet (0.5 to 3 m) tall. Woody stems are bristly or prickly, with shreddy yellow-brown bark. Leaves are alternate and pinnately compound, with three to five leaflets, green above and white or gray and hairy underneath. The native North American plant in that review is Rubus idaeus subsp. strigosus.

Season

Eat fruit when it is ripe on the plant. FEIS says it was eaten fresh or preserved for winter. It does not print one ripening month for the whole range.

Range

FEIS says it grows from Alaska through Canada to Newfoundland, south to North Carolina and Tennessee in the East, and to Arizona, California, and northern Mexico in the West. Cultivated plants have naturalized as well. A garden raspberry is the same species complex. A wild cane still has to match the features above.

Preparation

FEIS says the fruit was traditionally an important food, eaten fresh or preserved, and that the fruit is eaten fresh or in jams, jellies, and baked goods. Wash it. You do not need a special detox step for ripe fruit of this species in that review. Do not eat the leaves from this card. The review mentions medicinal preparations from fruit, root bark, and stems. This guide does not teach those.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The FEIS review used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this plant on a single identification. The fruit has to be the aggregate cluster on a bristly cane with the leaf shape above. A juicy berry on a thornless plant with different leaves is not this card. If any feature fails, leave it.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Before you eat any wild plant
pages.summary: Never eat a plant on a single identification. Poison hemlock, water hemlock, death camas, and yew are not food. Mushrooms are out.
pages.html:
Never eat a wild plant on a single identification. Use several features, from the plant in front of you, and reject it if one feature is wrong. A photo in this guide is not included in v0.1. Words are not enough when two species share a leaf shape. If you are not sure, do not eat it.

This guide does not cover mushrooms. Do not use it to identify a fungus.

Poison hemlock

USDA Agricultural Research Service says poison hemlock (Conium maculatum) grows through the United States and is extremely poisonous to people. All parts are poisonous: leaves, stem, fruit, and root. People are often poisoned after mistaking the root for wild parsnip, the leaves for parsley, or the seed for anise. Whistles made from the hollow stems have killed children. Do not eat any member of the carrot family from this guide. This guide has no wild-carrot card on purpose.

Water hemlock

ARS calls water hemlock (Cicuta, including Cicuta douglasii) the most violently toxic plant that grows in North America. A small amount can poison a person. The underground parts, especially the tuberous roots, are highly toxic. It has been confused with wild parsnips and other herbs. If you think someone has eaten it, contact a poison center and get emergency medical help. Do not wait for a field remedy. This guide gives none.

Death camas

ARS says death camas (Zigadenus species, also discussed now in Toxicoscordion) has grasslike leaves from a bulb and yellowish-white flowers. The bulbs are reported to cause severe illness and death in people. If a bulb was eaten, ARS says the effects may be lethal and the person needs emergency treatment. This guide does not teach wild onions. A bulb in the ground is not a free meal.

Yew

ARS describes yew (Taxus) as an evergreen shrub or small tree with narrow, stiff, pointed leaves about 1.25 to 2.5 cm long and a scarlet (sometimes yellow) fleshy fruit. Humans are susceptible. Taxine is the toxic alkaloid ARS names. Do not make tea from yew needles, and do not eat the fruit. This guide does not teach pine-needle tea. The pine pages in the Forest Service reviews used here describe wood or, for pinyon, seeds, not a needle tea, so a needle tea is not a technique this edition will invent. If you cannot tell a yew from another conifer, you are not making a drink out of either.

The plant cards that follow are foods only where a USDA or USFS page says so. Each card has its own deadly-look-alike block. Read that block before the preparation section.

pages.title: Blue elderberry
pages.summary: Only blue or purple berries. Red berries of other elderberry species are toxic. The plant contains alkaloids that can cause nausea.
pages.season: The USDA guide describes gathering clusters in July and August
pages.name: Blue elderberry
lookalikes: Red-berried elderberry species are toxic and should not be gathered
pages.html:
Identification

The USDA NRCS plant guide titled blue elderberry gives the name Sambucus nigra L. ssp. canadensis and the symbol SANIC4. It says recent taxonomy has moved and that the plant was previously split into several western names, including Sambucus caerulea, and is called Sambucus mexicana in some floras. Leaves are pinnately compound, with 2 to 4 paired leaflets plus a terminal leaflet, opposite each other on the branch. Flowers are white or cream. The berries this guide allows are blue or purple. Seedlings and shrubs without flowers or fruit can resemble California walnut and Oregon ash. Do not identify it from leaves alone.

Season

That guide says clusters are gathered in July and August in the California practice it describes, then dried or cooked. Do not pick red fruit and hope the month makes it safe.

Range

The guide is written around western riparian stands and the California floristic setting, including valley oak riparian habitat of the valley elderberry longhorn beetle. Do not treat this card as a license to eat every elderberry in the East. Check the USDA PLANTS map for the symbol, and still require blue or purple fruit on a plant you have identified with more than one feature. The beetle is federally listed. Do not cut occupied shrubs to get a snack.

Preparation

The guide says only the blue or purple berries are edible. They are made into wine, jam, syrup, and pies, and the guide also records drying and later cooking, and some dried fruit eaten without further cooking. It also says the active alkaloids hydrocyanic acid and sambucine will cause nausea, so care is required. Cook the berries. Do not eat leaves, bark, or red fruit. Folk-medicine uses of flowers, leaves, and juice are printed in that guide and are not taught here. There is no dose in this guide.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The USDA guide says the red berries of other elderberry species are toxic and should not be gathered. That is the deadly look-alike block. Never eat this plant on a single identification. If the fruit is red, or you are not sure it is blue or purple and ripe, do not eat it. If the shrub has no fruit and no flowers, the leaves are not enough, because the guide says they can resemble walnut and ash. Water hemlock is a separate deadly plant and does not look like a berry shrub. It is still a reason to stay out of unidentified wetland roots. Read the flora rules page.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Common dandelion
pages.summary: A basal rosette with a hollow, leafless flower stalk. Leaves are the food use documented here.
pages.season: Cool-season perennial; USFS records leaves eaten, without a narrower harvest calendar
pages.name: Common dandelion
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USFS dandelion review used here
pages.html:
Identification

The USFS FEIS review describes common dandelion as an introduced cool-season perennial. It has a thick taproot. Stems are very short and underground, so the leaves form a rosette on the ground. Leaves are about 2 to 16 inches (5 to 40 cm) long. Flower heads are solitary at the end of naked, hollow stalks that can reach about 2 feet (60 cm). One head can hold 100 to 300 flowers. Seeds sit under a parachute of bristles.

Season

FEIS does not print a month-by-month harvest chart. It is a cool-season plant, and the food note below is about the leaves. Do not assume a calendar the review does not give.

Range

pages.title: Broadleaf cattail
pages.summary: A wetland plant with a brown sausage spike. Several parts are edible at the right stage. Confirm every feature.
pages.season: Spring shoots about 4 to 16 inches; pollen when the spike is flowering; rhizomes described as a fall and winter food in ethnobotanical accounts cited by USFS
pages.name: Broadleaf cattail
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USDA cattail guide used here
pages.html:
Identification

The USDA NRCS plant guide (symbol TYLA) describes Typha latifolia as a herbaceous perennial in the cattail family, with rhizomes and long slender green stalks topped by brown, fluffy, sausage-shaped flowering heads. Plants are about 15 to 30 decimeters tall. The spike has staminate flowers above and pistillate flowers below. Basal leaves are thin with parallel veins running the long length of the leaf. Plants grow in colonies in wet ground.

Season

The guide says young shoots are cut from the rhizomes in spring when they are about 4 to 16 inches long. Pollen is used when the male flowers shed it. Rhizomes are the starch storage. Do not pull a green shoot from a plant that has no sausage spike you can tie to that same clump.

Range

The guide says broad-leaved cattails are common throughout the United States and in temperate and tropical places worldwide. Check the current USDA PLANTS map before you rely on a local stand. Wetland rules may prohibit digging.

Preparation

The guide says all parts are edible when gathered at the right stage. Young shoots can be eaten raw or steamed. The base of the stem where it meets the rhizome can be boiled or roasted. Young flower stalks, taken out of their sheaths, can be boiled or steamed. Pollen can stand in for flour. Rhizomes and lower stems can be eaten raw, baked, roasted, or broiled, and the core can be ground into flour. The guide's starch figures (about 30% to 46%, and a flour yield per acre) are citations inside that guide, not something you should expect from one plant.

Wash anything that grew in dirty water, and cook it if the water around the stand was not treated. The water module still applies to the water you boil them in.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The USDA guide used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this plant on a single identification. If there is no sausage-shaped flower head on the clump, and the leaves are not the long parallel-veined blades the guide describes, do not eat it. Flags, rushes, and bulrushes appear as alternate names in the guide. Those names are shared with other wetland plants. A shared nickname is a reason to stop, not a reason to eat.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Stinging nettle
pages.summary: Boiled leaves are eaten. The hairs sting. Do not eat it raw.
pages.season: Young stems in the growing season; always cook
pages.name: Stinging nettle
lookalikes: The plant's own stinging hairs injure skin; no separate deadly look-alike is named in the USFS review
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes stinging nettle as an erect perennial that forms dense clones. Stems are about 3.3 to 6.6 feet (1 to 2 m). Leaves, stems, and flowers are sparsely to moderately covered with stinging hairs. The fruit is an achene. American and hoary subspecies are native. European stinging nettle is introduced.

Season

FEIS does not give a month. Use leaves from the growing plant, and cook them. Gloves or a folded cloth keep the hairs off your skin while you pick.

Range

FEIS says American stinging nettle is the common subspecies through temperate North America: much of Canada and the United States, south in the East and Midwest to Virginia, Missouri, and Kansas, and in the West south along the coast to central California and in the Rockies to Mexico. European stinging nettle is mainly along the Atlantic coast from Newfoundland to Georgia and Alabama. It is listed as a noxious weed in several Canadian provinces. Harvest rules may apply.

Preparation

FEIS says boiled stinging nettle leaves are edible and can be substituted for spinach. Boil them. Do not eat them raw. The hairs are irritating to human skin, and the pollen is a hay-fever source. Medicinal uses are mentioned and are not taught here.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The FEIS review used here does not name a second species as a deadly look-alike. The hazard it does name is the plant itself. Stinging hairs hurt skin. Never eat this plant on a single identification, and never eat it uncooked. If the hairs and the upright clonal growth are not both there, it is not the plant in the review. A plant that only looks vaguely leafy is not nettle.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Lowbush blueberry
pages.summary: A low eastern shrub in colonies, with small sweet berries.
pages.name: Lowbush blueberry
lookalikes: No deadly look-alike is named in the USFS lowbush blueberry review used here
pages.html:
Identification

FEIS describes lowbush blueberry as an erect, low, variable shrub about 2 to 24 inches (5 to 60 cm) tall, usually in dense colonies. Roots are shallow. Flowers are in short racemes, terminal or axillary. The fruit is a globular berry about 0.12 to 0.4 inch (4 to 11 mm) across, larger on some cultivars, and FEIS calls the berries very sweet.

Season

Pick when the berries are ripe and sweet. FEIS does not give one month for the whole range.

Range

FEIS says it grows from Labrador and Newfoundland west to southern Manitoba and Minnesota, south to northern Illinois, and from New England through the Appalachians to West Virginia and Virginia. The state list on that review includes CT, DE, IA, IL, IN, ME, MA, MI, MN, NH, NJ, NY, NC, OH, PA, RI, TN, VT, VA, WI, and WV. A blueberry outside that pattern needs a different identification. Do not stretch this card to every blue berry in the West.

Preparation

FEIS says Native Americans ate the fruit fresh, dried, baked, in soups, or mixed with meat, and that settlers ate it fresh or in jams, jellies, and preserves. Wash the berries. No leaching step is described for the ripe fruit.

DEADLY LOOK-ALIKES

The FEIS review used here does not name a deadly look-alike. That is not a clearance. Never eat this plant on a single identification. The plant has to be the low colony-forming shrub with the berry FEIS describes. A blue berry on a tall plant, or a berry with a different calyx, is not this card.

Rule

Never eat on a single identification. When in doubt, do not eat it.

pages.title: Debris hut
pages.summary: A one-person wedge of sticks with a thick layer of dry leaves or needles.
pages.html:
Use this when you have leaves, needles, grass, or similar dry debris and you need warmth more than room. Both the FEMA appendix and FM 3-05.70 describe it. The Army manual calls it one of the better shelters for warmth when shelter is essential.

Shape:

  • Set a ridgepole with one end on a stump, log, or rock, or on a short tripod. The Army manual also allows anchoring the ridgepole to a tree at about waist height.
  • Lean sticks along both sides to make a wedge. It must fit your body and be steep enough to shed water.
  • Lay finer sticks and brush across the ribs so insulation does not fall through.
  • Heap on light, dry, soft debris.

How thick: the FEMA appendix says to push your arm through the debris to the ribs and have debris reach your armpit, and in cold weather to add another foot or two. FM 3-05.70 says at least 1 meter (3 feet), and thicker is better. Use the thicker of the two if you have the material. The Army manual also says to put about 30 centimeters (1 foot) of insulation inside, on the floor, and to keep a pile you can pull across the door once you are in. A layer of branches or shingles on the outside keeps the debris from blowing off.

Do not build it under the hazards on the site-selection page. Dead limbs overhead and a wash underfoot are not fixed by more leaves.

If the debris is wet, it will not insulate the way the manuals describe. Spend the effort looking for drier material under blown-down trees or on the lee side of a log rather than piling soaked leaves and calling it done.
