pages.title: Lean-to
pages.summary: A one-slope roof of a poncho or of poles, with the back into the wind.
pages.html:
A lean-to blocks wind and rain from one direction. It is not a closed hut. FM 3-05.70 describes two versions.

Poncho lean-to

The manual's materials are a poncho, about 2 to 3 meters (7 to 10 feet) of line, three stakes about 30 centimeters (1 foot) long, and two trees or poles about 2 to 3 meters apart. Check the wind first. The back of the lean-to faces the wind.

Tie the hood shut. Tie line to the two corner grommets on one long side, with a short stick on each line about 2.5 centimeters from the grommet so rain running down the line drips off instead of into the shelter. Tie those lines about waist high. Stake the other edge to the ground. For more than one night or for rain, add a center support so the roof does not sag into a puddle. Brush or a pack at the open sides cuts wind. Leaves or needles on the floor cut heat loss into the ground.

Pole lean-to

In woods, the same manual describes a lean-to of poles: a horizontal support about waist to chest high between two trees, beams rested on one side, and the back into the wind. It takes longer than a poncho roof. In cold weather the manual describes a green-log reflector wall on the fire side, filled with dirt so it throws heat. Only build a fire where it is legal and where you can keep it from the shelter and the duff. The Park Service says sparks melt and ignite tents; the same is true of a thatched roof.

A lean-to under a dead limb is still a bad site. Read the site page before you tie the first knot.

pages.title: Shelter priorities
pages.summary: In harsh weather, getting out of the wind and wet comes before food.
pages.html:
Exposure can hurt you faster than hunger. The FEMA US&R survival appendix says shelter is the critical necessity in that short course: you can last longer without water than you can last while exposed to a harsh environment, and it prints a teaching mnemonic of about 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in hypothermia conditions, 3 days without water, and 3 weeks without food. Treat that as their planning line, not a promise about your body.

The same appendix says to work one problem at a time, and to keep the shelter small. A smaller space takes less heat to warm. Put dry, airy debris between your body and the ground. Heat lost into cold ground is a real loss. Plastic can be a moisture barrier under that insulation, not a substitute for it.

U.S. Army FM 3-05.70 says a shelter has to be large enough to protect you and small enough to hold your body heat, especially in the cold. It also says to prefer a natural shelter you can alter, because building from nothing spends energy you may need later.

Order of work when the weather is the threat:

  • Get out of wind, rain, and standing water.
  • Insulate yourself from the ground.
  • Only then improve the roof, the door, and a way to signal.

Fire is not the first shelter. A fire you cannot keep inside a safe ring, or a fire under a snow-loaded branch, makes a second emergency. If you are with other people, one person can gather insulation while another picks a site that is not under a dead limb and not in a wash.

This page is not medical advice. Hypothermia care is on the first-aid page, and that page is still awaiting clinical review.

pages.title: Where not to camp
pages.summary: Look up for dead limbs, look down for flood paths, and stay off exposed peaks in a storm.
pages.html:
A bad site can wreck a good shelter. Check these before you commit.

Overhead wood

The National Park Service camping page says to look up: if you see dead branches overhead, do not camp under them, and stay away from dead trees that might fall. Sequoia and Kings Canyon add that branches and trees may fall whether or not they are dead, and when there is no wind. Do not linger under dead, cracked, broken, or hanging branches, or under trees rotten at the base or shedding cracked bark. People call hanging dead limbs widowmakers. The park warning is the same idea without needing the nickname.

FM 3-05.70 says to look for loose rocks, dead limbs, and other growth that could fall on a natural shelter.

Water and slope

The Park Service says to stay out of ravines that might flood, and FM 3-05.70 says to avoid flash-flood areas in the foothills and any site below the high-water mark. The FEMA appendix says to keep the shelter out of valleys, washes, troughs, and depressions, and to watch for avalanche slopes and rock that could collapse. FM 3-05.70 names avalanche and rockslide ground in the mountains as places to avoid.

Low ground is also colder at night. The Army manual says ravines, narrow valleys, and creek beds collect heavy cold air, and brushy low ground holds more insects.

Storms, cliffs, and animals

The Park Service says not to stay on ledges or high peaks where wind and lightning are the hazard, and to pick a spot sheltered and away from the middle of a field in a lightning storm and away from the edge of cliffs. In bear country that page says to keep about 200 feet between cooking and sleeping, store food at least 200 feet from where you sleep, and follow the park's food-storage rule.

The FEMA appendix also says to avoid poison oak, ant nests, and animal dens, and to keep the shelter away from the cooking fire.

Make camp while you can still see. The Park Service says to learn the ground in daylight.

pages.title: Snow trench, snow cave, and a snow mound
pages.summary: Get below the wind, keep a vent, and do not sleep on bare snow.
pages.html:
FM 3-05.70 says snow shelters work because snow insulates, and that building one takes time and gets you wet. Do this only when you have a digging tool and enough snow. Do not dig into an avalanche slope; the site page covers that hazard.

Snow trench

The manual's idea is to get below the snow and the wind. In compacted snow, cut blocks for a roof. If you cannot cut blocks, use a poncho or other sheet. Make one entrance and close it with a block or a pack.

Snow cave in a drift

Find a drift about 3 meters (10 feet) deep. Keep the roof arched so it is stronger and so melt runs down the sides instead of onto you. Build the sleeping platform higher than the entrance. Leave a gap, or a small trench, between the platform and the wall so melt does not soak you. This matters more if you have a heat source inside. The roof should be high enough to sit up on the platform. Close the entrance with a block. The manual says you can use the lower entrance area for cooking. Walls and ceiling should be at least 30 centimeters (1 foot) thick. Put in a ventilation shaft. A sealed snow hole can smother you. Keep the shaft open.

Mound you dig out

The same paragraph says that if you do not have a drift that deep, pile snow into a mound large enough to dig out. That mound-and-hollow shelter is the variation the manual gives. People often call a hollowed snow mound a quinzhee. The manual does not use that word and does not give a separate recipe, a wait time, or a diameter. Use the cave rules it does give: arched roof, sleeping platform above the entrance, thick walls and ceiling, and a ventilation shaft.

Tree-pit

Where evergreen trees grow, the manual says you can dig the snow out around a bushy trunk down to the depth you need or to the ground, pack the snow at the rim, lay boughs across the top, and put boughs under you. The tree is a roof only if it is not a hazard tree. A dead or cracked tree is not a good pit.

In every one of these, insulate your body from the snow you are lying on. Bare snow under you steals heat even when the roof is good.

The manual does not use that word and does not give a separate recipe, a wait time, or a diameter. Use the cave rules it does give: arched roof, sleeping platform above the entrance, thick walls and ceiling, and a ventilation shaft. ## Tree-pit Where evergreen trees grow, the manual says you can dig the snow out around a bushy trunk down to the depth you need or to the ground, pack the snow at the rim, lay boughs across the top, and put boughs under you. The tree is a roof only if it is not a hazard tree. A dead or cracked tree is not a good pit. In every one of these, insulate your body from the snow you are lying on. Bare snow under you steals heat even when the roof is good.

pages.title: Tarp and poncho setups
pages.summary: A sheet is a roof, a shade, or a ground cloth. Pitch the back to the wind and keep the edges from channeling rain inside.
pages.html:
A tarp, poncho, or similar sheet does not make heat. It sheds rain, cuts wind, or makes shade. Pair it with ground insulation from the priorities page.

Lean-to

See the lean-to page for the Army poncho lean-to: back to the wind, drip sticks on the ridge lines, stakes on the low edge, a center support if it will sag.

Low tent

FM 3-05.70 also describes a poncho tent between two trees about 2 to 3 meters apart, using two lengths of line and about six stakes. It covers both long sides and has a lower profile than a lean-to, with less room. Tie the hood the same way. A center prop or an A-frame over the middle keeps the roof off your chest. You still need a dry layer under you.

Desert shade

In dry country the manual says to spend effort carefully. If you have a poncho, canvas, or similar cloth, use a rock outcrop, a sand mound, or the gap between dunes. Anchor one end on the rock or the mound with weight, and stretch the other end so the cloth actually shades you. For a beach or open sand trench, it says to pick a site above the high-water mark, dig a trench long enough to lie in, running north to south so it takes less sun, mound the spoil on three sides, and lay driftwood or poles across as a roof frame. Grass or leaves make the bed, not the bare sand.

Ground cloth

The Park Service says a waterproof sheet under a tent works as a footprint if you fold the extra under. Cloth that sticks out past the tent floor collects rain and runs it underneath you.

Do not pitch any of these in a wash, under a widowmaker, or on a lightning-exposed peak. Those failures are on the site page, and a better knot will not fix them.

pages.title: Boiling
pages.summary: A rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 6,500 feet. Let it cool.
pages.html:
CDC calls boiling the best way to kill germs in water, including viruses, bacteria, and parasites such as Cryptosporidium and Giardia.

If the water is cloudy, strain it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter, or let it settle and pour off the clear water.

Then:

  1. 1. Bring the clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute.
  2. 2. Above 6,500 feet (about 1,981 meters), boil for 3 minutes.
  3. 3. Let it cool so you do not burn yourself.
  4. 4. Store it in a clean, covered container.

Boiling does not remove fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive material. If that is the problem, CDC says to use a different source.

A flat taste is normal. CDC says you can pour the water back and forth between clean containers and let it stand, or add a pinch of salt per quart or liter. That pinch is for taste, not a medical dose.

Boil water you will use for drinking, cooking, and brushing teeth when the only supply is untreated surface water. The hiking page says to boil even if you are not sure, and that filtering alone is not the first choice.

pages.title: Chlorine and iodine
pages.summary: Unscented household bleach can disinfect clear water. Iodine is a short-term backup with people who should not use it.
pages.html:
CDC says chemical disinfectants kill most germs but do not work as well as boiling against some parasites, including Cryptosporidium and Giardia. Chlorine bleach and iodine kill bacteria and viruses and do not work well on parasites. Chlorine dioxide tablets can kill Giardia and are somewhat effective on Cryptosporidium if you follow the label. Filter first when you can.

If the water is cloudy, murky, colored, or very cold, CDC says to double the bleach dose below. Strain or settle cloudy water first.

Use unscented household bleach. Do not use scented, color-safe, or bleach with added cleaners. Read the label. If it has drinking-water directions, follow those. If it does not, use the sodium hypochlorite strength on the label.

Bleach at 5% to 9%

CDC's emergency page, after stirring, wait at least 30 minutes:

  • 1 quart or liter: 2 drops (about 0.1 mL).
  • 1 gallon: 8 drops (about 1/2 mL, a little less than 1/8 teaspoon).
  • 5 gallons: 40 drops (about 2 1/2 mL, or 1/2 teaspoon).

Bleach at 1%

Same wait. This is more drops because the bleach is weaker:

  • 1 quart or liter: 10 drops (about 1/2 mL, or 1/8 teaspoon).
  • 1 gallon: 40 drops (about 2 1/2 mL, or 1/2 teaspoon).
  • 5 gallons: 200 drops (about 12 1/2 mL, or 2 1/2 teaspoons).

EPA's emergency page adds a check some kits use: after 30 minutes the water should smell slightly of chlorine. If it does not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes. If the chlorine taste is strong, pour the water between clean containers and let it stand.

Iodine

CDC says to follow the label on iodine tablets or drops. EPA describes one common backup: 5 drops of 2% tincture of iodine per quart or liter, or 10 drops if the water is cloudy or colored, then stand at least 30 minutes.

CDC says people who are pregnant, who have thyroid problems, or who are hypersensitive to iodine should not drink iodine-treated water. No one should drink it for more than a few weeks at a time.

Iodine and iodine tablets do not kill Cryptosporidium. Neither does chlorine alone. Boiling does.

These drop counts are disinfection instructions printed by CDC and EPA for emergency drinking water. They are not medicine doses for a person.

pages.title: Dew and a vegetation still
pages.summary: Cloth can wring dew. A plastic-sheet still is a slow backup, and boiling is still the surest germ kill.
pages.html:
These are small sources. They do not replace a treated creek when you have one.

Dew

The FEMA US&R appendix says rain can be caught on plastic and in any cup you set out, and that a blanket can be spread and wrung. It says dew can be collected the same way. Wring the cloth into a container. Then treat that water. Dew on a dirty cloth is not sterile, and CDC's rule is that you treat water unless you already know it is safe.

Sheet still

The same FEMA appendix describes a still: an open damp spot, a hole about 3 feet deep, a cup in the center, a plastic sheet about 6 by 6 feet sealed at the edges with the spoil, and a rock on the sheet so it sags over the cup. Moisture condenses on the underside and drips in. The appendix says vegetation or urine can be added to the hole. It also says the water collected this way is safe without further purification.

Read that next to CDC, which is the newer public-health page. CDC says boiling is the surest way to kill germs, and that you should not drink water that may hold fuel or chemicals. A dirty sheet, a cup that held something else, or fuel in the soil can contaminate condensate. If you can boil, boil what the still collects. Do not drink urine, and do not count on this hole for a group's daily water. The FEMA appendix's yield figure is not repeated here.

A bag tied over a live leafy branch is a transpiration bag. That method is not described in the FEMA appendix or the CDC pages used here, so this guide does not give bag sizes or wait times for it. Use the sheet still those pages do describe, or treat surface water.

pages.title: Filters
pages.summary: Most portable filters remove parasites. They do not remove viruses. Disinfect after you filter.
pages.html:
CDC's emergency page says portable filters do not remove all germs.

  • Viruses: a typical portable filter will not remove them.
  • Bacteria: the filter needs an absolute pore size of 0.3 micron or smaller.
  • Parasites such as Giardia and Cryptosporidium: absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller.

The hiking page says a filter labeled either of these removes parasites but not viruses, and not all bacteria:

  • absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller, or
  • certified to NSF standards 53 or 58 for cyst reduction or removal.

A 0.3 micron absolute pore size removes bacteria and parasites, not viruses. Reverse osmosis filters remove parasites, bacteria, and viruses, and also remove salt.

After filtering, CDC says to add a disinfectant (iodine, chlorine, or chlorine dioxide) so viruses and remaining bacteria are killed. The hiking page calls filter-then-disinfect the next best option after boiling. Boiling is still the surest single step.

Follow the manufacturer's instructions. A clogged or frozen filter does not meet the pore size you bought. Do not assume a coffee filter or a bandana is a germ filter. CDC lists cloth only as a way to remove cloudiness before the real treatment.

Filters do not make fuel or chemical contamination safe.

pages.title: Melt snow and ice before you drink it
pages.summary: Do not eat raw snow. Melt it, then treat the meltwater.
pages.html:
The FEMA appendix says eating raw snow can cause dehydration, and that ice is preferable to snow. Melt ice or snow in a pot over a fire or stove. Do not use body heat as the melter if you are already cold: that is the opposite of the shelter priority, which is to stop heat loss.

Meltwater is not automatically safe. Snow and ice sit where animals walk and where dust and soot land. CDC says clear water can still carry germs, and the emergency page's boil steps apply to water you have made clear. If the melt is cloudy, settle or strain it, then bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 6,500 feet.

Do not melt snow that is stained with fuel, dye, or unknown waste. CDC says boiling does not make fuel or toxic chemicals safe.

Yellow snow is not a joke and not a source. Pick clean snow away from camp trails and latrines, then still treat it.

pages.title: Solar disinfection (SODIS)
pages.summary: Clear water in clear bottles, on their side in the sun, for 6 hours or 2 days if cloudy.
pages.html:
CDC's emergency page says the sun can reduce the number of germs in water. It also says solar disinfection does not work well when the water is cloudy, because particles shade the germs.

Steps on that page:

  1. 1. If the water is cloudy, strain it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter, or let it settle and draw off the clear water.
  2. 2. Fill clean, clear plastic bottles with that clear water.
  3. 3. Lay the bottles on their side in the sun for 6 hours if it is sunny, or 2 days if it is cloudy. Laying them down exposes more water to the light. A dark surface under the bottles helps.

This is a backup when you cannot boil. It is slow, and it does nothing for fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive material. CDC says those waters need a different source.

Do not use a bottle that held chemicals. "Clear" means you can see through the plastic and the water. Colored bottles are not what the page describes.

Boiling remains the method CDC calls best. Use the sun when boiling is impossible, not as a shortcut past a stove you already have.

pages.title: Finding water without trusting how it looks
pages.summary: Clear water can still make you sick. Treat it, and do not drink water that may hold fuel or chemicals.
pages.html:
CDC's hiking page says germs from human or animal waste get into lakes, rivers, and streams, and that water can look clean and still be unsafe. Drinking straight from a clear mountain stream is given there as an example of something that is generally not safe. You can get sick from using untreated water to drink, cook, wash produce, make ice, or brush your teeth.

People at higher risk include children, pregnant people, adults 65 and older, and anyone with a weakened immune system. The illness CDC names from this kind of water is often diarrhea, vomiting, and stomach pain.

Boiling is the best way CDC gives to kill germs. The next best, on that page, is to filter and then disinfect the filtered water. Follow the label on any device you use.

If the water may contain fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive material, CDC says boiling and disinfecting will not make it safe. Use a different source. That includes flood water you cannot see through a chemical lens, and water from a radiator or boiler. The emergency page says never to use heating-system water for drinking, cooking, or hygiene.

Where you take water matters for the next person. If there is no toilet, CDC says to bury feces at least 8 inches deep and at least 200 feet from lakes, rivers, and other natural water, downstream of where people collect. Wash hands before food and after the toilet. If you have no soap and water, CDC says a sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol.

The boil, chemical, filter, and sun pages are the treatment steps. Do not skip them because the source "looks spring-fed."

pages.title: Springs, seeps, and moving water
pages.summary: A spring is still untreated water until you boil it or otherwise treat it.
pages.html:
A spring is groundwater coming to the surface. That sounds cleaner than a muddy creek. CDC does not give springs a pass. The hiking page says water that looks clean can hold bacteria, viruses, and parasites, and uses a clear mountain stream as the example. Treat spring water, seep water, and stream water the same way unless a land manager has posted that a specific tap or fountain is potable.

Prefer the clearest water you can reach, then make it clearer before treatment. CDC's emergency page says if water is cloudy, pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter, or let it settle and draw off the clear water. Then boil, or disinfect, or filter according to the method pages. Cloudy water blocks chemical treatment and sunlight.

Do not take water downstream of a carcass, a latrine, or an obvious chemical sheen. CDC says you cannot boil fuel or toxic chemicals out of water. Move upstream or use a stored supply.

In camp, keep the container you treat into clean, and cover it. The emergency page says to store boiled or disinfected water in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers.

This page does not list liters per day. The older kit notes in this repository use a planning floor that is not on the CDC pages cited here, so it is not repeated as a medical requirement.
